title: ACER: Accelerating Complex Event Recognition via Two-Phase Filtering under Range Bitmap-Based Indexes

problem.claim: Complex event recognition must identify specific patterns composed of several primitive events in event stores, where full scans incur costly I/O overhead.

gap.claim: Prior index-based approaches incur significant I/O and sorting overhead under high predicate selectivity or long query windows, causing high query latency.

contributions.claim: ACER is a Range Bitmap-based index for accelerating complex event recognition.
ACER groups same-type events into compressed clusters to reduce index space overhead and index-reading I/O.
ACER builds block-level Range Bitmaps with chronological ordering and uses merge operations plus two-phase window-condition filtering to avoid sorting and unnecessary disk access.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on six real-world and synthetic datasets reportedly show that ACER reduces query latency by up to one order of magnitude compared with state-of-the-art techniques.

narrative_sequence.summary: Complex event recognition identifies patterns composed of multiple primitive events in event stores.
Full scans create costly I/O overhead, while existing indexes suffer I/O and sorting overhead in demanding query conditions.
The paper proposes ACER, a Range Bitmap-based index.
ACER combines compressed same-type clusters, block-level Range Bitmaps, chronological ordering, merge operations, and two-phase filtering.
Experiments across six real-world and synthetic datasets report up to an order-of-magnitude query-latency reduction against state-of-the-art techniques.

source_observation.claim: The proposed index combines physical organization, ordered retrieval, and early filtering to reduce I/O and sorting costs.

interpretation.claim: Query performance can improve when storage layout and filtering strategy are designed together around the dominant execution costs.

application.claim: For event-store queries with selective predicates or long windows, consider clustered compression, ordered intermediate results, and condition-based early filtering.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether these design choices generalize beyond the reported datasets, workloads, or query conditions.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the detailed index construction algorithm or query execution procedure.
The abstract does not provide dataset characteristics, baselines, workload settings, or exact latency measurements beyond the maximum reported reduction.
The abstract does not report resource overheads other than index space overhead.
